messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Carlos, a 35-year-old Latin American male and musician, has been struggling with the aftermath of a life-threatening accident that occurred six months ago. The traumatic event involved a near-fatal car crash on a rainy night while he was returning from a gig. Despite his best efforts to recall the incident in detail, Carlos finds it difficult to access a clear narrative of what happened; memories come in disconnected pieces, leaving him with an incomplete picture. Carlos’s experience of the accident has led him to harbor deeply ingrained negative appraisals that shape his current behavior and coping strategies. He feels a profound sense of injustice, believing that nothing has been done about the unfairness he experienced. This belief, coupled with a fear that he might lose control of his anger and do something terrible, has led Carlos to adopt maladaptive strategies as a way to cope. He constantly surrounds himself with people, ensuring he is never alone with his thoughts. Socializing has become an almost compulsive habit for him; he seeks out gatherings, performances, and social events at every opportunity. This constant need for company helps mask the fragmented memories that persistently intrude on his mind. Each time Carlos tries to deliberately recall what happened, the memory becomes harder to access, reinforcing his avoidance of solitude. His wife has noticed a significant change in his behavior since the accident. He avoids talking about the event or its aftermath and often seems distracted during conversations, as if his mind is elsewhere. When he does attempt to discuss it, he quickly switches topics, unable to fully articulate what happened due to the fragmented nature of his memories. The difficulty Carlos experiences in recalling the event has compounded his negative appraisals. He feels that his life has been irrevocably destroyed by the trauma, and this belief further fuels his maladaptive strategies. The more he tries to avoid thinking about it, the harder it becomes to piece together a coherent narrative of what occurred. Over time, Carlos’s constant socializing has taken a toll on his relationships and work. He often cancels performances at short notice because the thought of being alone in the studio or backstage triggers intense anxiety. His wife has become increasingly concerned about his well-being and has noticed that he seems distant and preoccupied during their interactions. What finally brought Carlos to seek help was an incident where he became so overwhelmed by memories of the accident while playing a solo performance that he left the stage abruptly, much to the confusion and disappointment of his audience. This event highlighted for him how his maladaptive strategies were not only failing but also exacerbating his symptoms. Carlos is most afraid that he will never be able to recover from this trauma and live a normal life again. He hopes that through therapy, he can begin to process what happened in a more constructive way and regain control over his thoughts and behaviors. By understanding the interplay between his negative appraisals, memory difficulties, and maladaptive coping strategies, Carlos is taking an important step toward healing.
